newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: More jet fuel, diesel in storage ahead of winter.
newsitem.headline: More jet fuel, diesel in storage ahead of winter.

text.p: Oil companies are stocking up jet-kerosene fuel and diesel in the hope of bumper winter demand, industry sources said on Friday.
But not all their stock build-up is voluntary as some are left with little choice but to store excess supplies due to scarce prompt demand, traders said.

They said the large increase in middle distillate stocks in several storage terminals across the region--China, Guam, Singapore and the Middle East--led some to speculate that prices this winter might not rise as sharply as in previous years.

Last winter, jet fuel and diesel prices soared to trade at around $34.00 per barrel on a free-on-board (fob) Singapore basis, giving many storage players a decent profit, even though it was not as big as in 1995 amid a severe winter.
The prompt weakness has led to a steep contango--where the present value of the product is much cheaper than the forward price.
The contango, which exceeds $4.00 per barrel, sufficiently pays for the four or five months that the companies have to keep the oil products in storage, they said.
It costs about 50 cents to store one barrel of middle distillate for a month in most of the regional independent storage terminals, traders said
The current price of jet-kerosene fuel is around $22.60 pre barrel, compared to $26.50 in the fourth quarter and $27.20 in the first quarter of 1998, brokers said.
Diesel prices are also in contango but at a narrower level with the current price at $22.90, compared to $24.50 in the fourth quarter and $24.90 in the first quarter, brokers said.

One trader said such high stocks are also found in other independent storage terminals across Asia, with some estimating total middle distillate stocks in storage tanks for "winter play" at over 10 million barrels.
Industry sources said the current winter play might not yield the same dividend as in past years due to the large increase in refining capacity since last year.
In 1996, Asian refining capacity grew by 1.2 million barrels-per-day (bpd) to 18.1 million bpd.
The increase in storage of middle distillates is clearly seen from the release of weekly stock data from the Singapore Trade Development Board.

Middle distillate stocks in Singapore, which includes jet-kerosene fuel and diesel, have consistently hovered between 10 and 12 million barrels over the past months--its highest levels in over three weeks.
Normal average stocks are between six and eight million barrels.

Last winter, even though the amount of arbitrage exports from the West to East Asia were much lower than in 1995, the higher refining output and products stored for the cold season were enough to meet the peak demand, they said.
Middle distillate demand soars in winter, as North Asian countries, especially Japan and South Korea, raise consumption of the two products for heating fuel.
